sections.title: Front matter

summary.text: Presents the front matter of the WHO interim guidance Digital Documentation of COVID-19 Certificates: Vaccination Status (DDCC:VS) — Technical Specifications and Implementation Guidance (27 August 2021, WHO/2019-nCoV/Digital_certificates/vaccination/2021.1), including copyright and licensing notices, the table of contents, acknowledgements, abbreviations, a glossary of technical and data-protection terms, and the Executive Summary. The Executive Summary defines the DDCC:VS as a digitally signed HL7 FHIR representation of COVID-19 vaccination events supporting two primary scenarios (Continuity of Care and Proof of Vaccination) across paper and digital formats without requiring a smartphone, and outlines the minimum policy, data, and service requirements (including Health Certificate Identifiers, a Generation Service, and a Registry Service).

sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduces Section 1 by framing the global COVID-19 pandemic context and the need for countries to provide verifiable records of COVID-19 vaccination status that augment fraud- and loss-prone paper cards while respecting human rights, equity, ethical considerations, and data protection principles.

sections.extract: Coronavirus disease (COVID-19), caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), was first identified in December 2019 and has spread to become a global pandemic. The outbreak has forced curtailment of movement, curfews and adoption of preventative measures to try to halt transmission, lower the burden on health systems, and reduce morbidity and loss of life. COVID-19 vaccines are being

sections.title: Purpose of this document

summary.text: States the purpose of the document in Section 1.1: to provide a software-agnostic baseline set of requirements, a core data set, and a digital-signature approach based on free and open standards so Member States can design, adapt, and deploy interoperable DDCC:VS solutions in paper-plus-barcode or digital formats.

sections.extract: This document lays out an approach for creating a signed digital version of a vaccination record for COVID-19 based on a core data set of key information to be recorded, and an approach for the digital signature. The document leverages existing free and open standards, and is driven by the ethics, use cases and requirements for Digital Documentation of COVID-19 Certificates: Vaccination Status (DDCC:VS). summary.text: Identifies the primary target audience in Section 1.2 as national authorities responsible for creating or overseeing COVID-19 digital vaccination certificate solutions, along with supporting government partners, international organizations, NGOs, local businesses, and trade associations.

sections.extract: The primary target audience of this document is national authorities tasked with creating or overseeing the development of a digital vaccination certificate solution for COVID-19. The document may also be useful to government partners such as local businesses, international organizations, non- governmental organizations and trade associations, that may be required to support Member States in developing or deploying

sections.title: Scope

summary.text: Defines the in-scope and out-of-scope boundaries in Section 1.3: in-scope elements cover ethical and data-protection principles, Continuity of Care and Proof of Vaccination use cases, the core data set, the HL7 FHIR implementation guide, and national trust framework considerations, whereas SARS-CoV-2 test and infection/recovery certificates, immunity-passport policy decisions, AEFI reporting, rollout monitoring, country-specific 2D barcode identity-binding algorithms, and selective disclosure functionality are out of scope.

sections.extract: 1.3.1. In scope This document specifically focuses on how to digitally document COVID-19 vaccination status and attest that an individual has received a vaccine (i.e. how to provide a signed digital vaccination certificate). Two priority scenarios are described in Table 1: Continuity of Care and Proof of Vaccination. This document describes a specification for a signed digital vaccination certificate, including:

sections.title: Assumptions

summary.text: Outlines the foundational assumptions in Section 1.4 regarding Member States' responsibilities in setting up and operating a DDCC:VS solution, including legal and human-rights compliance, preventing digital exclusion via paper-and-barcode support indexed by a Health Certificate Identifier (HCID), establishing a national Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) with root and document signer certificates (DSCs) not tied to individual health workers, and operating DDCC:VS Generation, Registry, and optional Repository services.

sections.extract: The technological specification for a DDCC:VS is intended to be flexible and adaptable for each Member State to meet its diverse public health needs as well as the diverse needs of individuals around the world. It is assumed that there is no one-size-fits-all solution, and so the specification must remain flexible and software-agnostic, while minimizing the amount of digital infrastructure required. sections.title: Ethical considerations and data protection principles

summary.text: Introduces Section 2 by emphasizing that ethical considerations—such as equity and equitable access—and data protection principles must inform both the technical design criteria and national deployments of any DDCC:VS solution.

sections.extract: SECTION 2 As with any digital solution, there are ethical considerations, such as potential impacts on equity and on equitable access, and data protection principles that need to inform the design of the technical specifications, as well as provide guidance on how resulting solutions can be ethically implemented. The following sections discuss some key ethical considerations and data protection principles that

sections.title: Ethical considerations for a DDCC:VS

summary.text: Details the ethical considerations for designing and deploying a DDCC:VS in Section 2.1, examining public health objectives (promoting welfare, preventing health inequities and digital exclusion, and maintaining public trust), procedural values (transparency, inclusiveness, accountability, and responsiveness), ethical risks of 'health pass' uses amid scientific uncertainties and unequal vaccine access, and six core recommendations for domestic implementation.

sections.extract: This section presents ethical considerations to take into account when designing, developing and deploying a DDCC:VS as part of the response to the COVID-19 pandemic (which may be extended to other diseases). This document covers two priority scenarios of use for a DDCC:VS, which are: 1. as a record to serve as the basis for continuing healthcare for that individual (Continuity of Care); and 2. as a record

sections.title: Data protection principles for a DDCC:VS

summary.text: Establishes seven fundamental data protection principles for DDCC:VS in Section 2.2 to guide national authorities and safeguard privacy and human rights: lawful basis, legitimate use and fair processing; transparency; purpose limitation and specification; proportionality, necessity and data minimization; confidentiality and security (including breach notification); data subject rights, complaint and legal redress; and independent oversight and accountability.

sections.extract: This section presents fundamental data protection principles for the DDCC:VS as a prerequisite for continuity of care and proof of vaccination. The principles are designed to provide guidance to the national authorities tasked with creating or overseeing the development of the DDCC:VS. The objectives are to encourage Member States to adopt or adapt their national laws and regulations, as necessary, respect personal

sections.title: DDCC:VS core data set

summary.text: Introduces Section 5 on the DDCC:VS core data set, explaining that it comprises the critical Subject of Care and vaccination-event data elements required for interoperability across the Continuity of Care and Proof of Vaccination scenarios, either used directly or mapped from existing terminologies, with a full data dictionary provided in Web Annex A.

sections.extract: SECTION 5 SECTION DDCC:VS core data set 5 The DDCC:VS core data set includes data elements about the Subject of Care and vaccine administration events that are required for the two core scenarios of Continuity of Care and Proof of Vaccination. sections.title: Core data set principles

summary.text: Outlines the core data set principles in Section 5.1—data minimization, open standards, implementability on both paper and digital formats, and integration with broader immunization information systems (EIRs, DHIS2, Vigiflow)—and recommends HL7 FHIR (based on the International Patient Summary) and ICD-11 as the preferred open standard and terminology system, with ICD-10, ATC, and SNOMED CT GPS mappings supported.

sections.extract: To develop the core data set, data requirements under the International Health Regulations (15), WHO home-based records guidance (13), WHO adverse events following immunization (AEFI) reporting requirements (26) and WHO immunization programme monitoring guidance are considered (12). The core data set has been further informed by analysis of existing digital vaccination certificates deployed in some countries and by

summary.text: Defines the DDCC:VS core data elements in Section 5.2 across three tables: Table 10 (header section identifying the Subject of Care: name, date of birth, unique identifier, and sex), Table 11 (vaccination event data for each dose: vaccine/prophylaxis, brand, manufacturer or market authorization holder, batch number, vaccination date, valid-from date, dose number, total doses, country, administering centre, health worker signature or ID, targeted disease, and next-dose due date), and Table 12 (certificate metadata: issuer, HCID, certificate validity dates, and schema version). It also introduces Section 6 on the National Trust Architecture and PKI chain of trust (Figure 13) for signing and verifying a DDCC:VS.

sections.extract: The three key sections of the core data set are: 1. the header 2. data elements for each vaccination event 3. vaccination certificate metadata. The header section data elements include the Subject of Care’s ID information (see Table 10). The header section is intended to capture information about the vaccinated individual to allow for information on the vaccination event to be linked to a specific person. This data

sections.title: Signing a DDCC:VS

summary.text: Explains the three-step process for digitally signing a DDCC:VS in Section 6.1 (illustrated in Figure 14): generating a root certificate key pair, signing Document Signer Certificate (DSC) key pairs with the root private key, and hashing the vaccination data and signing the document hash with the DSC private key.

sections.extract: The process of signing a DDCC:VS is shown in the top row of Fig. 13 and involves three steps. 1. The PHA generates a private and public key pair that serve as the “root certificate”. The private key is kept highly secure (never revealed to another party, maintained in a disconnected location, stored on media that is itself password-protected, etc.); the public key will be widely disseminated. 2. The PHA generates

sections.title: Verifying a DDCC:VS signature

summary.text: Describes the four-step process for verifying a DDCC:VS digital signature in Section 6.2 (illustrated in Figure 15), where a Verifier computes the document hash, reads the signed hash, decrypts it using the DSC public key to confirm data integrity and signer authenticity, and validates the DSC signature using the PHA's root certificate public key.

sections.extract: The verification process, shown in in the bottom row of Fig. 13 and further detailed in Fig. 15, reverses the signing process to verify content in the signed DDCC:VS. 1. A Verifier calculates its own hash (i.e. “calculated hash”) from the information in the DDCC:VS using the same hashing algorithm as was used by the document signer. 2. The DDCC:VS’s signed hash is read by a digital solution. 3. The document signer’s

sections.title: Trusting a DDCC:VS signature

summary.text: Explains the mathematical and operational basis for trusting a DDCC:VS signature in Section 6.3, noting how asymmetric cryptography guarantees authenticity and non-repudiation while PKI provides trusted public-key distribution and key revocation mechanisms.

sections.extract: The cryptographic strength of private–public key pairs is based on the mathematics of asymmetric cryptography, a process involving “one-way” mathematical functions, which are operations that are easy to compute in one direction but extremely hard to reverse. They provide a high level of security provided the private key is not compromised and remains available only to the entity performing the signing.

summary.text: Introduces Section 8 on implementation considerations, contrasting two strategic approaches for Member States: deploying a short-term DDCC:VS solution with a defined sunset roadmap for the COVID-19 emergency versus building a long-term digital vaccination certificate infrastructure that supports routine immunization records and broader digital health initiatives.

sections.extract: SECTION Implementation considerations 8 Since COVID-19 was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern under the IHR in January 2020, there has been a clear and urgent need for all Member States to effectively address the COVID-19 pandemic. summary.text: Details key factors for Public Health Authorities to consider when procuring and partnering with external solution developers in Section 8.2, including clear terms of reference, fixed-price versus time-and-materials contracts, realistic phased timelines, single supplier versus consortium models, measurable KPIs, supplier expertise and project management track records, communication and cultural alignment, long-term partnership potential, and intellectual property and software licensing rights.

sections.extract: The solution discussed in this document involves applying digital signatures to information to provide a guarantee that the information has been validated by an accredited authority. The proposed method is to employ a digital certificate using a private–public key pair, a common mathematical approach for encryption and digital trust.
